rows.question: What does 21 CFR 820.10 require?
rows.answer: 21 CFR 820.10 requires that a manufacturer subject to this part must document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable requirements of this part. The manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 of this chapter, if applicable, and procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of part 821 of this chapter, if applicable, and notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter. Advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter. The requirements in Design and Development apply to class II, class III, and those class I devices listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section. Devices automated with computer software must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. The devices listed in the following table must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. Devices that support or sustain life must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements in this part, as appropriate. The failure to comply with any applicable requirement in this part renders a device adulterated under section 501(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Such a device, as well as any person responsible for the failure to comply, is subject to regulatory action. [4][5]

rows.question: What does 21 CFR Part 11 cover?
rows.answer:
21 CFR Part 11 covers the requirements for electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records. It sets forth the criteria under which the agency considers electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records to be trustworthy, reliable, and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures executed on paper.

- [1] Each electronic signature shall be unique to one individual and shall not be reused by, or reassigned to, anyone else.
- [2] Persons who use closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, when appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records, and to ensure that the signer cannot readily repudiate the signed record as not genuine. Such procedures and controls shall include the following:
  - [4] Electronic signatures that are not based upon biometrics shall:
  - [5] For records required to be maintained but not submitted to the agency, persons may use electronic records in lieu of paper records or electronic signatures in lieu of traditional signatures, in whole or in part, provided that the requirements of this part are met.
- [6] The regulations in this part set forth the criteria under which the agency considers electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records to be trustworthy, reliable, and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures executed on paper.
- [7] Persons who use open systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, as appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of their creation to the point of their receipt. Such procedures and controls shall include those identified in § 11.10, as appropriate, and additional measures such as document encryption and use of appropriate digital signature standards to ensure, as necessary under the circumstances, record authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality.
- [8] The definitions and interpretations of terms contained in section 201 of the act apply to those terms when used in this part.

- [10] Electronic signatures and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records shall be linked to their respective electronic records to ensure that the signatures cannot be excised, copied, or otherwise transferred to falsify an electronic record by ordinary means.

rows.question: Summarize FDA guidance FDA-2016-D-2565.
rows.answer: The FDA guidance FDA-2016-D-2565 outlines requirements for the Third Party Review Program and Third Party Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) Review. It specifies that industry, food and drug administration staff, and third party review organizations must submit electronic comments for consideration to the FDA at [1]. The guidance also states that comments may not be acted upon until the document is revised or updated. Additional copies are available from the Internet. The guidance includes nonbinding recommendations for the 3P510k Review Program and Third Party EUA Review, covering factors used in determining device eligibility, the assignment of reviewers, and the substantive review process. These requirements are based on the source [1].

rows.question: What records must a device manufacturer keep for complaints?
rows.answer: The device manufacturer must keep records that include information evaluated to determine if an event was reportable, all medical device reports and information submitted to the FDA, any information evaluated for preparing annual reports, and systems that ensure access to information for timely follow-up and inspection. These records must be documented in written MDR procedures, located in a separate section, and describe how investigations are conducted. If the manufacturer ceases marketing the device, they still have an obligation to report adverse events involving the device. If the manufacturer purchases a device under 510(k), they remain obligated to report adverse events for the devices they manufactured. The packaging and labeling of the devices should identify the manufacturer with corresponding address and contact information. If the manufacturer agrees to assume responsibility for reporting adverse events, a written agreement should be documented. The requirement applies to all devices manufactured and distributed by the manufacturer. [1] [2]
citations: FDA Guidance: Medical Device Reporting for Manufacturers : Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff (final, 2016-11-08, Docket FDA-2013-D-0743)
